transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello, Doctor. It's nice to meet you. I'm... well, I'm here because things have been just a bit stressful lately at work. I've been on the production line for years, you know, just doing my job, keeping my head down, but recently they asked me to start helping out with the safety trainings for the new hires. Which is nice, I suppose, it's good to be recognized for knowing the ropes, but... well, it's just that when I'm up there, pointing at the diagrams or demonstrating the equipment, I just... I can't stop staring at my hands. They just look so incredibly wrinkly, and the skin tone is all uneven, and I feel like everyone is just staring at how old and awful my hands look when I'm trying to show them what to do. It's all I can focus on. And then, because of the trainings, they took some photos for the company newsletter, and when I saw them, I swear my face looks completely crooked. Like, one side is just drooping or pulling wrong, and my jaw looks lopsided. I brought it up to my sister, and even a couple of the girls on the line, and they all just brush it off and say they don't see it, that I look fine, but I know what I'm seeing. It's just... it's really starting to bother me, you know? I can't stop thinking about it, even when I'm just trying to relax at home. It's just so distracting.
How much do these concerns about your hands and face bother you when you're not at work or thinking about the photos?

Well, it's... I mean, it's not like I'm sitting in the dark crying about it or anything dramatic like that. I still get my chores done and all. But, you know, even when I get home from the plant, I'll take off my work boots, put my feet up, and sit down with a cup of tea to watch my evening programs—I usually watch Jeopardy and Wheel of Fortune, just to unwind, you know? And I'll just be resting my hands on my lap, not doing anything at all, and my eyes just go right to them. I'll catch the lamplight hitting my knuckles and I just start turning them over, looking at the spots and the way the skin gathers, and I can't help but think about how they looked pointing at those safety charts earlier in the day. 

And then with the face thing... well, I'll go into the bathroom to wash up before bed, just my normal routine, washing up with a bit of cold cream like I've done since I was a young woman, and I end up just leaning way over the sink, staring at my jawline in the mirror. I'll turn my head this way, then that way, trying to see if it really is as crooked as it looked in that newsletter picture. I'll spend I don't know how long just pulling at my cheeks a little, trying to see if maybe the skin is just sagging on one side or if the bone is actually lopsided. 

It doesn't stop me from getting my sleep, and I still do my grocery shopping on the weekends and keep the house tidy, so I'm getting by. But it's just this constant, nagging thought. Like a pebble in your shoe, I guess? It's just always sort of there in the back of my mind, bothering me, even on a Sunday when I'm nowhere near the factory and haven't looked at a photo in days.
Do you find yourself worrying about other parts of your body, or is it mostly your hands and face that concern you?

Well, it's really just the hands and the face, mostly the jawline like I was saying. I mean, goodness, at my age, you know there are plenty of things that aren't quite what they used to be. My knees ache when it rains, and I certainly don't have the figure I had when I was twenty-five and going out dancing on the weekends, but I don't really fret over those things. That's just getting older, isn't it? You expect gravity to take its toll on your waistline, and I wear my coveralls at work anyway, so who's looking? 

But the hands... they're right out there in front of me all day, pulling levers, checking the line, and now pointing at those safety boards. And the face, well, that's what everyone looks at when you're talking to them. I don't sit around worrying about my stomach or my arms or my feet or anything like that. I just wash my hair, put it up in a clip, and that's fine. It's really just... it's just this crookedness in my jaw that I saw in that photo, and how incredibly old and spotted my hands look. I'll be at the grocery store pushing the cart, and I'll just stare at my hands gripping the handle, thinking about how they must look to the cashier when I hand over my money. But no, I don't go looking in the mirror at the rest of me, picking it apart. Just the hands and the face. That's more than enough to be getting on with, honestly.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly, like checking mirrors, touching your face, or taking photos to examine your appearance?

Well, yes, I suppose I do, now that you mention it. It's... well, it's mostly when I have to be in front of people, like I was saying about the safety trainings. Or even if I'm just heading down to the senior center for one of those little workshops they put on—I like to go to the gardening ones, they're quite lovely, but even then, I get so anxious about how I look. 

Before I have to go stand up there or sit with a group, I'll always make a quick trip to the ladies' room. I just... I have to check the mirror. And I don't just glance, I'll stand there and turn my head side to side, you know, trying to catch the light just right to see if that crookedness in my jaw is as obvious as I think it is. I'll tilt my chin up, then tuck it down, just really studying it. And my hands... oh, I carry this little bottle of hand lotion in my purse—it's a chamomile one, very soothing—and I'll just rub it in, over and over, hoping it might plump up the skin a bit or make the wrinkles look less deep. I'll put it on, and then I'll look at them under the harsh bathroom lights, and sometimes I'll put a little more on. 

And then, well, I hate to admit it because it feels a bit silly at my age, but sometimes I'll catch one of the other girls on the line, like Brenda or Susan—Susan's been there almost as long as I have—and I'll just casually ask, "Do I look alright?" or "Does my face look a bit swollen on this side today?" And they always say I look fine, just like my sister does, but I just need to hear it, I guess. 

Between the mirror checking, the lotion, and tracking down Susan to ask her opinion, I do end up running a few minutes late sometimes. Not terribly late, mind you! I'm not missing the trainings or skipping the workshops. I always get myself there, and I do my job, but it does make me feel a bit rushed and flustered, having to do all that just to feel okay enough to walk into the room. It's just a whole routine I never used to have to do, and it takes up time, you know?
Do you ever avoid certain situations, like speaking in front of others or going out in public, because you're worried about how your hands or face look?

Well, avoid... I wouldn't say I completely avoid things altogether. I mean, I haven't stopped working or volunteering or anything drastic like that. I still punch the clock every morning, and I still help out at the church rummage sale every spring, sorting the donations and pricing the knick-knacks just like I've done for years. 

But... well, it does slow me down, like I was saying about getting ready for those safety trainings. I used to just grab my clipboard and walk right into the conference room, maybe pour a cup of that awful breakroom coffee on the way. Now, it’s a whole ordeal. I have to go to the ladies' room first, check the mirror, reapply my chamomile lotion, figure out where to stand in the room so the fluorescent lights don't cast such harsh shadows on my jaw... it just takes me so much longer to feel ready to stand up there in front of everyone. 

And photos? Oh, my goodness, I absolutely duck out of those now. If someone pulls out a smartphone—and everyone has them now, always snapping pictures of every little thing without even asking—I just sort of slide to the back of the group or pretend I need to go check on something on the line. Just last month it was Dave's retirement party—he worked in shipping for forty years, wonderful man, always had a joke to tell—and they wanted a big group picture with his sheet cake. I just couldn't do it. I slipped away to the kitchen to fetch more napkins just so I wouldn't have to see my lopsided face and spotted hands pinned up on the company bulletin board again. 

And even just regular social things... I hesitate now. I really do. I used to just say yes right away if the girls wanted to grab a bite at the diner after our shift on a Friday. Now, I pause. I think about sitting in that booth, under those bright lights, and having them look at my face while I'm talking, or seeing my hands holding the menu, and I second-guess the whole thing. I usually still go, but I don't enjoy the lead-up to it like I used to. It's like I have to really talk myself into it first, whereas before I would have just grabbed my purse and gone.
Do these concerns about your hands and face ever make it hard for you to focus on your work, sleep, or enjoy activities you used to like?

Well, it's a lot like what I was just telling you, really. It hasn't stopped me from working or doing my volunteering at the church—I still get up and punch the clock every single day, and I still do my shifts at the rummage sale. And my sleep is mostly fine, thank goodness, because if I didn't get my seven hours I'd be no use to anyone on the production line! I mean, unless my husband is snoring, which sounds like a freight train coming through the bedroom, but that’s a whole different story. 

But as for focusing and actually enjoying the things I used to like... yes, that's where it really gets to me. Like I was saying just a moment ago about being so slow getting ready for those trainings, or how I've started ducking out of photos and hesitating before I go out with the girls on Fridays. I used to just love those diner trips so much. They have this wonderful cherry pie, and Susan and Brenda and I would just sit in that booth and laugh for hours about absolutely nothing. But now, even when I do force myself to go, I can't fully enjoy it because my mind just isn't on the conversation. It's on my jawline. I'm sitting there wondering if the overhead lights are making my face look crooked, instead of actually listening to Susan talk about her grandchildren. 

And at work, it definitely messes with my focus. I'll be inspecting the parts on the line—we make these little brass valves, you see, and you have to be very careful to check the threads to make sure they aren't stripped—and I'll look down at my hands holding the valve, and I just lose my train of thought completely. I'll just stare at the wrinkles and those awful brown spots, wondering if the new floor manager, Mr. Henderson, noticed how old my hands looked when he handed me my daily quota sheet that morning. 

So, I'm still doing everything. I haven't quit my life or hidden away in my house or anything drastic like that. But it just takes the shine off it all, you know? It’s always right there in the back of my head, making everything feel like so much more work than it used to be, and making it so hard to just be in the moment and enjoy myself.
Do you think other people notice or pay a lot of attention to the way your hands or face look?

Well, that’s the frustrating part of it all, and honestly, it’s the main reason I finally decided to come in and see someone like you in the first place. Because, well, ever since I started helping out with those safety trainings I was telling you about—which I only agreed to do because Mr. Henderson practically begged me, seeing as I know the production floor layout better than anyone else on the shift—I just can’t seem to stop noticing how terribly wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I’m up there pointing things out. I'll be standing there, pointing at the diagrams for the emergency shut-off valves, and my mind just races, thinking that every single pair of eyes in that conference room is glued to the brown spots and the loose skin on my knuckles. 

And then, oh, they take these pictures for the company newsletter. They put it out every quarter, printed on this thick, glossy paper that just highlights every little flaw, and they always include a little section on the safety meetings. I look at those photos and I just start thinking my face looks so horribly crooked. The whole jawline just looks completely lopsided to me, like one side is just sagging right off my skull. 

But here is the thing that really gets me, and it answers your question, I suppose... when I actually ask people about it, they tell me I'm imagining things. Like I mentioned with Susan on the line, or even my husband when I bring the newsletter home and set it on the kitchen table—I'll point right at the picture and say, "Look at how crooked my jaw is there," and they swear up and down they don't see it. My husband just sighs and tells me I look exactly the same as the day he married me, which is sweet but obviously not true, we were twenty-two! But they all insist they don't see the unevenness or the crookedness at all. So, I don't know if they're just being polite because they care about me and don't want to hurt an old woman's feelings, or if they genuinely aren't paying attention to it. But even though other people say they don't see it, it feels so obvious to me that I just assume everyone must be staring at it the second I walk into a room.

Do you ever feel that the way your hands or face look is not just a normal part of aging, but something that makes you appear disfigured or deformed in a way that others should notice, even if they say they don't?

Well, exactly, that’s just it. That’s exactly why I’m sitting in this chair right now, like I was just telling you. I mean, I know I’m sixty-four years old. I’m not a fool, I don’t expect to look like one of those young girls working the front reception desk who just graduated high school last year. I know what normal aging looks like. Susan has wrinkles, Brenda has age spots... we've all been working on that line for decades, it takes a toll. But when I look at myself, it feels like so much more than just getting older. 

Like I said, the whole reason I finally made this appointment and came in was because since I started doing those safety trainings, I just absolutely cannot stop noticing how extremely wrinkly and completely uneven my hands look when I’m pointing things out on the board. It doesn't look like a normal older woman's hands to me, it looks... well, yes, deformed is a strong word, but honestly, that's exactly how it feels! It feels like they are abnormally weathered and misshapen, like something is actually wrong with them. 

And it’s the exact same thing with my face. I know I keep bringing up those newsletter photos, but it's because it just haunts me. When I look at those pictures, I don't just see a woman getting a little older and getting some smile lines. I start thinking my face looks so severely crooked, like the actual bone structure of it is just fundamentally wrong or disfigured. 

And it just makes me feel like I'm completely isolated, because, like I was just saying a minute ago, I'll point it out to my husband or the girls at the diner and they swear up and down they don’t see it! They tell me it's just normal, or that I look fine. But how can it be normal if one side of my jaw looks completely lopsided compared to the other? It’s just so incredibly frustrating when you feel like there is this glaring, horrible defect on your own body, something that makes you look entirely abnormal, and everyone else is just acting like you're making a mountain out of a molehill.
Have you ever thought that the way your face or hands look might be caused by a medical condition or something wrong with your body that a doctor should check out?

Oh, a medical condition? Like a disease or an illness or something? No, no, I've never really thought it was anything like that. I mean, I don't sit there at the kitchen table looking at my hands and think, "Oh, I must have some sort of terrible skin disease or a bone disorder," heaven forbid. My cousin Martha had a bone issue a few years back, and that was just a terrible ordeal, she had to go all the way up to the state hospital for treatments, and I wouldn't wish that on my worst enemy. 

But no, with my hands and my jaw, I just think it's... well, it's just how I'm aging, but in this completely awful, exaggerated, disfigured way. Like I just got the absolute short end of the stick when it comes to getting older. I don't think I need to go see Dr. Miller—he's my general practitioner, wonderful man, he actually delivered both of my nephews—I don't think I need to go down to his office and ask for a blood test or an x-ray or anything like that. Because what's he going to do? There's no pill for having a lopsided jaw or hands that look like they belong on a hundred-year-old witch, you know? 

It’s not an illness, it’s just... me. It's just my face and my skin being completely misshapen. I know my blood pressure is fine, my cholesterol is finally down after I stopped eating those fried onion rings at the diner—Susan still gets them every single Friday, and I honestly don't know how her heart handles it, bless her—so physically, internally, I know I'm as healthy as a horse for a woman my age. I can still stand on the production line for eight hours without my knees giving out! 

It's just the outside. The outside is what's entirely wrong. So no, I've never thought it was a medical problem that a regular doctor needed to check out or cure. It just feels like a horrible physical defect that I'm stuck with, and that everyone has to stare at whenever I'm up there pointing at those safety diagrams. It's just my own ugly cross to bear, I suppose, not a sickness.
Do these concerns about your hands and face ever make you feel so self-conscious that you have trouble functioning normally in your daily life, like at work or when you’re out in public?

Well, you know, it hasn't completely stopped me in my tracks, if that's what you mean. I haven't quit my job or anything like that. I still go down to the plant every day, clock in at 6:00 AM sharp just like I have for the last twenty-two years, and I still do the safety trainings. Mr. Henderson would be absolutely lost if I stopped doing them, he really would. He relies on me so much for those. And I still go to the diner with Susan and Brenda, and I still go to church on Sundays. So, I am still functioning, I suppose you could say. 

But... well, it does make things harder. It really does. Like with the safety trainings, for instance. I used to just grab my clipboard and walk right into the conference room, no problem. But now, oh goodness, it takes me so much longer to get ready. I'll be in the ladies' room for twenty minutes before the meeting, just washing my hands over and over, putting lotion on them, trying to rub it in a certain way to see if it plumps up the skin and hides the wrinkles, adjusting my collar to see if it shadows my jawline differently... Susan actually came in looking for me last Tuesday because I was taking so long, she thought I'd fallen ill! 

And the photos, well, I've just started outright ducking out of them whenever I can. When they bring that camera out for the newsletter, I suddenly remember I have to check on the pressure gauges on line four, or I'll just step behind Mr. Henderson so only the top of my head shows. I just can't bear the thought of my crooked face being printed on that glossy paper again for everyone in the breakroom to stare at. 

And even just going out... I used to love our Friday nights at the diner, or going to the church potlucks. I'd just throw on a nice blouse and go. But now, I hesitate. I really do. I'll stand by the front door with my purse, just agonizing over whether people are going to be looking at my hands when I pass the casserole dish, or if the fluorescent lights in the diner are going to highlight how lopsided my jaw is. I still go, usually, because my husband practically pushes me out the door, bless his heart, but it's just not as easy or as enjoyable as it used to be. It's like this heavy weight I have to carry with me everywhere I go, constantly worrying about who is noticing how awful I look.

Would you say these worries about your hands and face cause you a level of distress or interfere with your life enough to be considered clinically significant, or do you feel it's still within a normal range of concern?

Well, "clinically significant," I don't really know how you doctors measure that, to be perfectly honest with you. I don't know the medical cut-offs for these things. But if you're asking if it's just a normal range of concern... no, I don't think it's normal at all. 

Like I was just explaining a minute ago, it hasn't stopped me from working my shifts or doing my volunteering. I still help out with the church food drive every single Thanksgiving, I've done that for fifteen years and I'm not about to let Pastor Davis down now, and I certainly haven't missed a single one of my safety meetings at the plant. I push through it. But it's just... it's the heavy toll it takes on me to actually do those things now. 

I'm so much slower getting ready for the trainings because I'm just agonizing over my hands in the mirror, and I've completely started ducking out of any photos they try to take of us for the newsletter or the bulletin board. And those social events I used to just love and go to without a second thought? Now I'm hesitating at the door. I really am. I'll stand there with my hand on the doorknob, second-guessing if I should even go inside because I feel so awful about how my lopsided face is going to look to everyone in the room. 

It hasn't paralyzed me, thank the Lord, I'm still moving forward. But it's changed how I live my day-to-day life. I used to enjoy going out and being around people so much more easily, and now everything just feels like this exhausting chore because of this constant, nagging worry about my appearance. So if that's what you mean by significant—that it's getting in the way of me just living simply and happily—then yes, doctor, it's definitely significant to me.

I'll tilt my chin up, then tuck it down, just really studying it. And my hands... oh, I carry this little bottle of hand lotion in my purse—it's a chamomile one, very soothing—and I'll just rub it in, over and over, hoping it might plump up the skin a bit or make the wrinkles look less deep. I'll put it on, and then I'll look at them under the harsh bathroom lights, and sometimes I'll put a little more on. 

And then, well, I hate to admit it because it feels a bit silly at my age, but sometimes I'll catch one of the other girls on the line, like Brenda or Susan—Susan's been there almost as long as I have—and I'll just casually ask, "Do I look alright?" or "Does my face look a bit swollen on this side today?" And they always say I look fine, just like my sister does, but I just need to hear it, I guess. 

Between the mirror checking, the lotion, and tracking down Susan to ask her opinion, I do end up running a few minutes late sometimes. Not terribly late, mind you! I'm not missing the trainings or skipping the workshops. I always get myself there, and I do my job, but it does make me feel a bit rushed and flustered, having to do all that just to feel okay enough to walk into the room. It's just a whole routine I never used to have to do, and it takes up time, you know?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient avoids certain situations due to concerns about appearance, which would support social anxiety or body dysmorphic disorder.
doctor.question: Do you ever avoid certain situations, like speaking in front of others or going out in public, because you're worried about how your hands or face look?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It hasn’t stopped me from working or volunteering, but I’m slower getting ready for trainings and I’ve started ducking out of photos or hesitating before social events I used to enjoy more easily.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the concerns cause the patient to avoid situations like public speaking or going out, which directly relates to functional impairment and avoidance behaviors.

patient.answer:
Well, avoid... I wouldn't say I completely avoid things altogether. I mean, I haven't stopped working or volunteering or anything drastic like that. I still punch the clock every morning, and I still help out at the church rummage sale every spring, sorting the donations and pricing the knick-knacks just like I've done for years. 

But... well, it does slow me down, like I was saying about getting ready for those safety trainings. I used to just grab my clipboard and walk right into the conference room, maybe pour a cup of that awful breakroom coffee on the way. Now, it’s a whole ordeal. I have to go to the ladies' room first, check the mirror, reapply my chamomile lotion, figure out where to stand in the room so the fluorescent lights don't cast such harsh shadows on my jaw... it just takes me so much longer to feel ready to stand up there in front of everyone. 

And photos? Oh, my goodness, I absolutely duck out of those now. If someone pulls out a smartphone—and everyone has them now, always snapping pictures of every little thing without even asking—I just sort of slide to the back of the group or pretend I need to go check on something on the line. Just last month it was Dave's retirement party—he worked in shipping for forty years, wonderful man, always had a joke to tell—and they wanted a big group picture with his sheet cake. I just couldn't do it. I slipped away to the kitchen to fetch more napkins just so I wouldn't have to see my lopsided face and spotted hands pinned up on the company bulletin board again. 

And even just regular social things... I hesitate now. I really do. I used to just say yes right away if the girls wanted to grab a bite at the diner after our shift on a Friday. Now, I pause. I think about sitting in that booth, under those bright lights, and having them look at my face while I'm talking, or seeing my hands holding the menu, and I second-guess the whole thing. I usually still go, but I don't enjoy the lead-up to it like I used to. It's like I have to really talk myself into it first, whereas before I would have just grabbed my purse and gone.

inference.note: The patient does not meet full criteria for F32.0 (Major Depressive Disorder, single episode) as there is no evidence of depressed mood, anhedonia, or other core depressive symptoms. The focus remains on appearance concerns, repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, reassurance seeking), and avoidance of photos/public situations due to perceived flaws, which supports the ongoing consideration of body dysmorphic disorder (F45.21). Social anxiety (F40.1) remains relevant due to performance anxiety in front of others, but not a primary delusional preoccupation (ruling out F22.0 for now).

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in functioning due to concerns about appearance, beyond what has already been described.
doctor.question: Do these concerns about your hands and face ever make it hard for you to focus on your work, sleep, or enjoy activities you used to like?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It hasn’t stopped me from working or volunteering, but I’m slower getting ready for trainings and I’ve started ducking out of photos or hesitating before social events I used to enjoy more easily.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the impact of the symptoms on work, sleep, and enjoyment of activities, which directly maps to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, it's a lot like what I was just telling you, really. It hasn't stopped me from working or doing my volunteering at the church—I still get up and punch the clock every single day, and I still do my shifts at the rummage sale. And my sleep is mostly fine, thank goodness, because if I didn't get my seven hours I'd be no use to anyone on the production line! I mean, unless my husband is snoring, which sounds like a freight train coming through the bedroom, but that’s a whole different story. 

But as for focusing and actually enjoying the things I used to like... yes, that's where it really gets to me. Like I was saying just a moment ago about being so slow getting ready for those trainings, or how I've started ducking out of photos and hesitating before I go out with the girls on Fridays. I used to just love those diner trips so much. They have this wonderful cherry pie, and Susan and Brenda and I would just sit in that booth and laugh for hours about absolutely nothing. But now, even when I do force myself to go, I can't fully enjoy it because my mind just isn't on the conversation. It's on my jawline. I'm sitting there wondering if the overhead lights are making my face look crooked, instead of actually listening to Susan talk about her grandchildren. 

And at work, it definitely messes with my focus. I'll be inspecting the parts on the line—we make these little brass valves, you see, and you have to be very careful to check the threads to make sure they aren't stripped—and I'll look down at my hands holding the valve, and I just lose my train of thought completely. I'll just stare at the wrinkles and those awful brown spots, wondering if the new floor manager, Mr. Henderson, noticed how old my hands looked when he handed me my daily quota sheet that morning. 

So, I'm still doing everything. I haven't quit my life or hidden away in my house or anything drastic like that. But it just takes the shine off it all, you know? It’s always right there in the back of my head, making everything feel like so much more work than it used to be, and making it so hard to just be in the moment and enjoy myself.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient's concerns about appearance are associated with a preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws that are not observable or appear slight to others, which is key in differentiating Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.21) from other conditions.
doctor.question: Do you think other people notice or pay a lot of attention to the way your hands or face look?

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
target_item.manifestation: I came in because since I started helping with the safety trainings, I can’t seem to stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I’m pointing things out, and then I start thinking my face looks crooked in the newsletter photos even though other people say they don’t see it.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks if other people notice or pay attention to the patient's perceived flaws, which directly maps to the aspect of S067 regarding defects being 'not observable or appear slight to others'.

patient.answer:
Well, that’s the frustrating part of it all, and honestly, it’s the main reason I finally decided to come in and see someone like you in the first place. Because, well, ever since I started helping out with those safety trainings I was telling you about—which I only agreed to do because Mr. Henderson practically begged me, seeing as I know the production floor layout better than anyone else on the shift—I just can’t seem to stop noticing how terribly wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I’m up there pointing things out. I'll be standing there, pointing at the diagrams for the emergency shut-off valves, and my mind just races, thinking that every single pair of eyes in that conference room is glued to the brown spots and the loose skin on my knuckles. 

And then, oh, they take these pictures for the company newsletter. They put it out every quarter, printed on this thick, glossy paper that just highlights every little flaw, and they always include a little section on the safety meetings. I look at those photos and I just start thinking my face looks so horribly crooked. The whole jawline just looks completely lopsided to me, like one side is just sagging right off my skull. 

But here is the thing that really gets me, and it answers your question, I suppose... when I actually ask people about it, they tell me I'm imagining things. Like I mentioned with Susan on the line, or even my husband when I bring the newsletter home and set it on the kitchen table—I'll point right at the picture and say, "Look at how crooked my jaw is there," and they swear up and down they don't see it. My husband just sighs and tells me I look exactly the same as the day he married me, which is sweet but obviously not true, we were twenty-two! But they all insist they don't see the unevenness or the crookedness at all. So, I don't know if they're just being polite because they care about me and don't want to hurt an old woman's feelings, or if they genuinely aren't paying attention to it. But even though other people say they don't see it, it feels so obvious to me that I just assume everyone must be staring at it the second I walk into a room.

inference.note: The patient continues to demonstrate preoccupation with perceived physical defects (hands and face), repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, seeking reassurance), and significant distress and functional impairment (interference with work, social activities, and enjoyment of hobbies). There is no evidence of delusions, ruling out F22.0 definitively. The differential remains between F40.1 (social anxiety disorder) and F45.21 (body dysmorphic disorder), with increasing support for F45.21 given the detailed focus on appearance, checking behaviors, and reassurance seeking.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concerns about her appearance are focused exclusively on perceived physical defects (e.g., wrinkles, crooked jaw) or if there is an underlying belief involving delusional thinking about her appearance.
doctor.question: Do you ever feel that the way your hands or face look is not just a normal part of aging, but something that makes you appear disfigured or deformed in a way that others should notice, even if they say they don't?

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
target_item.manifestation: I came in because since I started helping with the safety trainings, I can’t seem to stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I’m pointing things out, and then I start thinking my face looks crooked in the newsletter photos even though other people say they don’t see it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the severity of the perceived flaws (whether the patient feels disfigured or deformed) and the belief that others should notice them, which directly addresses the core symptom of being preoccupied with perceived defects in appearance.

patient.answer:
Well, exactly, that’s just it. That’s exactly why I’m sitting in this chair right now, like I was just telling you. I mean, I know I’m sixty-four years old. I’m not a fool, I don’t expect to look like one of those young girls working the front reception desk who just graduated high school last year. I know what normal aging looks like. Susan has wrinkles, Brenda has age spots... we've all been working on that line for decades, it takes a toll. But when I look at myself, it feels like so much more than just getting older. 

Like I said, the whole reason I finally made this appointment and came in was because since I started doing those safety trainings, I just absolutely cannot stop noticing how extremely wrinkly and completely uneven my hands look when I’m pointing things out on the board. It doesn't look like a normal older woman's hands to me, it looks... well, yes, deformed is a strong word, but honestly, that's exactly how it feels! It feels like they are abnormally weathered and misshapen, like something is actually wrong with them. 

And it’s the exact same thing with my face. I know I keep bringing up those newsletter photos, but it's because it just haunts me. When I look at those pictures, I don't just see a woman getting a little older and getting some smile lines. I start thinking my face looks so severely crooked, like the actual bone structure of it is just fundamentally wrong or disfigured. 

And it just makes me feel like I'm completely isolated, because, like I was just saying a minute ago, I'll point it out to my husband or the girls at the diner and they swear up and down they don’t see it! They tell me it's just normal, or that I look fine. But how can it be normal if one side of my jaw looks completely lopsided compared to the other? It’s just so incredibly frustrating when you feel like there is this glaring, horrible defect on your own body, something that makes you look entirely abnormal, and everyone else is just acting like you're making a mountain out of a molehill.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient believes their perceived physical defects are due to a medical or neurological condition.
doctor.question: Have you ever thought that the way your face or hands look might be caused by a medical condition or something wrong with your body that a doctor should check out?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient attributes their perceived flaws to an underlying medical condition, which relates to somatic concerns or delusional beliefs. The remaining symptom profile item (S068) covers appearance-related repetitive behaviors like checking mirrors and seeking reassurance, not medical attributions.

patient.answer:
Oh, a medical condition? Like a disease or an illness or something? No, no, I've never really thought it was anything like that. I mean, I don't sit there at the kitchen table looking at my hands and think, "Oh, I must have some sort of terrible skin disease or a bone disorder," heaven forbid. My cousin Martha had a bone issue a few years back, and that was just a terrible ordeal, she had to go all the way up to the state hospital for treatments, and I wouldn't wish that on my worst enemy. 

But no, with my hands and my jaw, I just think it's... well, it's just how I'm aging, but in this completely awful, exaggerated, disfigured way. Like I just got the absolute short end of the stick when it comes to getting older. I don't think I need to go see Dr. Miller—he's my general practitioner, wonderful man, he actually delivered both of my nephews—I don't think I need to go down to his office and ask for a blood test or an x-ray or anything like that. Because what's he going to do? There's no pill for having a lopsided jaw or hands that look like they belong on a hundred-year-old witch, you know? 

It’s not an illness, it’s just... me. It's just my face and my skin being completely misshapen. I know my blood pressure is fine, my cholesterol is finally down after I stopped eating those fried onion rings at the diner—Susan still gets them every single Friday, and I honestly don't know how her heart handles it, bless her—so physically, internally, I know I'm as healthy as a horse for a woman my age. I can still stand on the production line for eight hours without my knees giving out! 

It's just the outside. The outside is what's entirely wrong. So no, I've never thought it was a medical problem that a regular doctor needed to check out or cure. It just feels like a horrible physical defect that I'm stuck with, and that everyone has to stare at whenever I'm up there pointing at those safety diagrams. It's just my own ugly cross to bear, I suppose, not a sickness.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning due to concerns about their appearance, which would help differentiate between BDD (F45.21) and a more general anxiety or adjustment issue.
doctor.question: Do these concerns about your hands and face ever make you feel so self-conscious that you have trouble functioning normally in your daily life, like at work or when you’re out in public?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It hasn’t stopped me from working or volunteering, but I’m slower getting ready for trainings and I’ve started ducking out of photos or hesitating before social events I used to enjoy more easily.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the impact of the patient's concerns on her daily functioning, work, and social life, which maps directly to the Functional Impairment item.

patient.answer:
Well, you know, it hasn't completely stopped me in my tracks, if that's what you mean. I haven't quit my job or anything like that. I still go down to the plant every day, clock in at 6:00 AM sharp just like I have for the last twenty-two years, and I still do the safety trainings. Mr. Henderson would be absolutely lost if I stopped doing them, he really would. He relies on me so much for those. And I still go to the diner with Susan and Brenda, and I still go to church on Sundays. So, I am still functioning, I suppose you could say. 

But... well, it does make things harder. It really does. Like with the safety trainings, for instance. I used to just grab my clipboard and walk right into the conference room, no problem. But now, oh goodness, it takes me so much longer to get ready. I'll be in the ladies' room for twenty minutes before the meeting, just washing my hands over and over, putting lotion on them, trying to rub it in a certain way to see if it plumps up the skin and hides the wrinkles, adjusting my collar to see if it shadows my jawline differently... Susan actually came in looking for me last Tuesday because I was taking so long, she thought I'd fallen ill! 

And the photos, well, I've just started outright ducking out of them whenever I can. When they bring that camera out for the newsletter, I suddenly remember I have to check on the pressure gauges on line four, or I'll just step behind Mr. Henderson so only the top of my head shows. I just can't bear the thought of my crooked face being printed on that glossy paper again for everyone in the breakroom to stare at. 

And even just going out... I used to love our Friday nights at the diner, or going to the church potlucks. I'd just throw on a nice blouse and go. But now, I hesitate. I really do. I'll stand by the front door with my purse, just agonizing over whether people are going to be looking at my hands when I pass the casserole dish, or if the fluorescent lights in the diner are going to highlight how lopsided my jaw is. I still go, usually, because my husband practically pushes me out the door, bless his heart, but it's just not as easy or as enjoyable as it used to be. It's like this heavy weight I have to carry with me everywhere I go, constantly worrying about who is noticing how awful I look.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concerns about her appearance meet the threshold for causing clinically significant distress or impairment in functioning, which would support BDD over a phobia or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Would you say these worries about your hands and face cause you a level of distress or interfere with your life enough to be considered clinically significant, or do you feel it's still within a normal range of concern?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It hasn’t stopped me from working or volunteering, but I’m slower getting ready for trainings and I’ve started ducking out of photos or hesitating before social events I used to enjoy more easily.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the worries cause clinically significant distress or interfere with daily life, which directly maps to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, "clinically significant," I don't really know how you doctors measure that, to be perfectly honest with you. I don't know the medical cut-offs for these things. But if you're asking if it's just a normal range of concern... no, I don't think it's normal at all. 

Like I was just explaining a minute ago, it hasn't stopped me from working my shifts or doing my volunteering. I still help out with the church food drive every single Thanksgiving, I've done that for fifteen years and I'm not about to let Pastor Davis down now, and I certainly haven't missed a single one of my safety meetings at the plant. I push through it. But it's just... it's the heavy toll it takes on me to actually do those things now. 

I'm so much slower getting ready for the trainings because I'm just agonizing over my hands in the mirror, and I've completely started ducking out of any photos they try to take of us for the newsletter or the bulletin board. And those social events I used to just love and go to without a second thought? Now I'm hesitating at the door. I really am. I'll stand there with my hand on the doorknob, second-guessing if I should even go inside because I feel so awful about how my lopsided face is going to look to everyone in the room. 

It hasn't paralyzed me, thank the Lord, I'm still moving forward. But it's changed how I live my day-to-day life. I used to enjoy going out and being around people so much more easily, and now everything just feels like this exhausting chore because of this constant, nagging worry about my appearance. So if that's what you mean by significant—that it's getting in the way of me just living simply and happily—then yes, doctor, it's definitely significant to me.

inference.note: The patient's preoccupation with perceived physical defects limited to specific body parts (face and hands), along with repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, reassurance seeking) and clinically significant distress and functional impairment, supports the diagnosis of body dysmorphic disorder (F45.21). Other candidates (F22.0, F40.1) are ruled out based on absence of symptoms consistent with delusional disorder or specific phobia.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a persistent preoccupation with perceived defects in her hands and face, specifically wrinkles, uneven skin tone, and a crooked jawline, which she believes make her appear disfigured. These concerns are not better explained by another mental disorder, such as a mood disorder or a delusional disorder (no fixed delusions or depressive symptoms), and meet criteria for Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD), as evidenced by repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, excessive grooming, reassurance seeking), significant distress, and mild functional impairment related to social and occupational situations.
